title: The Night Bus to Bouaké
author: Léxi
desc: Un bus de nuit, onze passagers, et une valise qui disparaît. Qui ment ?

p: The night bus leaves Abidjan at ten p.m. It is going to Bouaké. The trip takes five hours.
Inspector Mariam Touré is not working tonight. She is going to visit her mother. She sits in seat number 4, by the window, with a book and a bag of plantain chips.
There are eleven passengers. Mariam looks at them, because police officers always look at people.

A businessman with a grey suitcase that he never lets go. A young couple who argue in low voices. An old pastor with a Bible. A student with headphones. A woman with a sleeping baby. A tall man in sunglasses — at night. And four market women who laugh and share bread.
The bus starts. The lights of Abidjan disappear behind them. Mariam opens her book and, slowly, she falls asleep.
At one o'clock in the morning, a scream wakes everybody up.
"My suitcase! My suitcase is gone!"
It is the businessman. His grey suitcase is not under his seat anymore. He is red in the face. "There are ten million francs in it! Stop the bus! Nobody leaves!"
The driver stops the bus on the side of the road. Around them, there is only the dark forest and the sound of insects.
Mariam stands up and shows her police card. "I am Inspector Touré. Everybody stays in their seat, please."
She asks questions. The businessman, Mr. Assi, says he slept for twenty minutes. Before that, the suitcase was there.
"So the suitcase disappeared in the last twenty minutes," says Mariam. "And the bus didn't stop. So it is still here."
Mariam talks to every passenger.
The young couple were arguing about money. "We have debts," says the girl, crying. Suspicious.
The tall man in sunglasses says he is a musician. He wears sunglasses because his eyes hurt. He has a big guitar case. Very suspicious.
The student says he heard nothing, because of his headphones. But Mariam sees that his headphones are not connected to anything.
The pastor says he was praying. The market women say they were sleeping. The mother says her baby cried at half past twelve, and she walked to the back of the bus to calm him.
"Did you see anything at the back?" Mariam asks her.
The woman hesitates. "Only the driver's assistant. He was moving bags."
Everybody looks at the tall man's guitar case. He opens it slowly. Inside, there is… a guitar. Only a guitar.
The driver's assistant, a young man called Lassina, says he moved bags because one fell. "I touched nothing else, I swear!"
Mariam walks slowly down the bus. She looks under the seats. She looks at the floor. Then she stops next to the pastor.
"Pastor, your Bible is very big," she says.
"The word of God is big, my daughter," he says, smiling.
"May I see it?"
The pastor stops smiling.
Mariam opens the Bible. It is not a real book. Inside, the pages are cut, and there is a hole. In the hole, there are many little bags of money, and a small key.
"This key opens the suitcase, doesn't it?" says Mariam.
But the pastor does not run. He looks at Mr. Assi, the businessman.
"Tell them, Assi. Tell them where the money comes from."
Mr. Assi becomes very pale.

The pastor explains. His real name is Joseph. He is not a pastor. He is a teacher from a village near Bouaké. Mr. Assi took money from the village to build a school. He never built the school. He kept the money.
"Tonight he was taking the money to hide it," says Joseph. "I followed him. I only wanted to take back what belongs to the children."
The bus is silent. The market women look at Mr. Assi with angry eyes.
Mariam thinks for a long time. Then she makes two phone calls. One to the police in Bouaké, for Mr. Assi. And one to the head of the region's schools, about the money.
"Joseph, stealing is still stealing," she says. "But I will tell the judge your story."
At five in the morning, the night bus arrives in Bouaké. The sun rises, orange and gold. And for the first time in years, a small village is going to get its school.
